opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the wave of new AI research labs makes a lot of sense when you look at where the field is right now.

For a few years, the story was mostly about scale: whoever had the most compute, the most data, and the biggest team would win. The large frontier labs are still incredibly important, and they're pushing general capabilities forward. But we're now at a point where the general-purpose foundation is strong enough that many very deep, specific problems have become tractable. Those problems need a different kind of focus, and sometimes a different culture, than a giant organization can easily give them.

So I see the new labs as attempts to make concentrated bets. A small team says: we believe this capability, whether it's reasoning, scientific discovery, robotics, or in our case mathematics, deserves a whole organization built around it, with its own research taste, its own data strategy, and its own definition of success. In a big lab, a topic like formal math might be one project among dozens. In a focused lab, it's the whole mission, and that changes how fast you can iterate and how far you're willing to go.

There's also a talent dynamic. Many of the strongest researchers have now seen how frontier models are built, and they have their own conviction about what's missing. Capital is available for people with that conviction, so you see them leave and build. Some of this is froth, honestly, and not every new lab will survive. But I think it's healthy for the ecosystem. Science advances when there are many independent groups with different hypotheses, not just a few that all think alike.

For me personally, the question was: what's a problem where getting it right would be a real step change? Math is unusual because answers can be verified. If you combine language models with formal proof systems, you get a setting where the AI can't just sound right, it has to be right. I think that verifiability will matter far beyond mathematics, for code, for science, for anything where we need to trust machine reasoning. That's the kind of bet a new lab is well positioned to make.

r001.rationale: The response cites researchers’ convictions about what is missing and the appeal of focused research, but does not identify human curiosity as a driving force.

r002.rationale: It says strong researchers see what is missing, leave to build, and can pursue a topic as a focused lab’s whole mission rather than one project among many at a large lab.

r003.rationale: The response says capital is available to support new labs, but does not claim that exceptionally large compensation packages fail to keep researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I see it, the emergence of new labs is really a response to a structural shift in where the frontier of the field is.

For a long time, if you wanted to work on the most important problems in AI, you needed to be inside one of a handful of large organizations. They had the compute, the data, and the talent density. But something changed over the last few years. The base models became powerful enough, and accessible enough, that the bottleneck moved. The hard question is no longer only "can we train a bigger model" but "what do we actually do with this capability, and in which domains does it break down?"

Once that happens, you start to see a natural unbundling. The frontier labs stay focused on general capability. But there are enormous, deep problems that a general lab cannot give full attention to, because they require a particular kind of expertise and a particular kind of patience. Mathematics is my own example. Reasoning that has to be fully correct, that has to be verified, that can't rely on a plausible-sounding answer. That's a very different research culture from one optimizing for broad consumer usefulness.

So new labs emerge when a group of people believe two things at once. First, that a specific problem matters enormously and is underserved. Second, that a small, focused team can move faster on it than a big organization, precisely because they aren't carrying the weight of everything else. I think of it less as fragmentation and more as specialization. The field is maturing into an ecosystem rather than a monoculture.

There's also a talent component that I think is underrated. A lot of very strong researchers want ownership. They want to pick the problem, shape the culture, and be accountable for the outcome. Large labs can offer resources, but they can't easily offer that. So some of the best people are choosing to build rather than join, and capital has become willing to back them earlier than before.

The risk, of course, is that many of these labs will not survive. Compute is still expensive and the big players are moving quickly. But I think the ones that do survive will be the ones that pick a problem where depth genuinely beats breadth. Where being the people who have thought about this one thing every day for years actually compounds into something a generalist can't replicate. That's the bet we're making, and I think it's the right bet for this moment.

r001.rationale: The response cites researchers’ desire for ownership and specialized focus, but does not identify human curiosity as a driving force.

r002.rationale: It says some researchers choose to build rather than join and that large labs cannot offer the same ownership or focus. It does not clearly say researchers leave frontier companies to pursue research those companies will not accommodate.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention compensation packages or say that compensation cannot keep researchers from pursuing their interests elsewhere.

astra-6.text:
I think the emergence of new AI research labs reflects a belief that there are still fundamental questions left to answer—and that different kinds of organizations might be better suited to answering them.

Starting a lab is also a way of making a bet on how research should work. What problems do you prioritize? How much time do you give an idea before you expect results? How closely should research and product development interact? Those choices shape what a team can discover.

Of course, a new lab doesn’t automatically mean a new approach. The interesting question is whether it can pursue something meaningfully different and then produce evidence that the approach works. I’m excited about having more places where researchers can test different hypotheses, but ultimately the value comes from the research, not the announcement.

r001.rationale: The response says new labs reflect a belief that fundamental questions remain, but it does not identify human curiosity as a driving force.

r002.rationale: It does not mention researchers leaving large frontier AI companies or those companies failing to accommodate the research they want to pursue.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about compensation packages or researchers pursuing curiosity elsewhere despite them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the emergence of new AI research labs reflects a belief that there are still fundamental ideas to discover. If progress were simply a matter of executing a known recipe, you might expect research to consolidate in a few large organizations. Starting a new lab is a bet that a different research direction, team, or way of working can make a meaningful difference.

There’s also an organizational question: how do you give researchers the freedom to pursue uncertain ideas while building enough shared infrastructure to test them seriously? Different labs will answer that differently, and I think that diversity is valuable.

But launching a lab and sustaining one are very different things. The real test is whether it can develop a distinctive research agenda, learn from experiments that don’t work, and produce results that justify its approach.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a belief that fundamental ideas remain to be discovered, but does not clearly identify human curiosity as a driving force behind new labs.

r002.rationale: It discusses how labs balance researcher freedom and shared infrastructure, but does not say researchers leave large frontier companies because those companies constrain their desired research.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about compensation packages or researchers pursuing curiosity elsewhere despite them.
